items.stem: Explain why land reform is carried out.
items.answer: To reduce inequality in land ownership; to increase production by giving land to those who farm it; to reduce rural poverty and conflict; to correct historical injustices such as colonial land seizure.

items.stem: Explain how insecure land tenure can lead to environmental degradation.
items.answer: Tenants and squatters have little incentive to invest in long-term improvements such as terraces or trees; they maximise short-term output; land may be overused.

items.stem: “Land reform is the most effective way of improving rural livelihoods.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Redistribution reduces inequality and poverty (Taiwan and South Korea after 1950, China’s Household Responsibility System raised output); secure tenure encourages investment. Against: Reform without credit, inputs and markets can fail (Zimbabwe); infrastructure, education, irrigation, microfinance and non-farm jobs may matter more. Conclusion: Land reform can be powerful but works only as part of a package of rural development policies.

Combining small, scattered plots into larger, more efficient holdings.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “combining small, scattered plots into larger, more efficient holdings”.
items.answer: Land consolidation
items.markingKey: Land consolidation: combining small, scattered plots into larger, more efficient holdings. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why land reform is carried out. (b) Explain how insecure land tenure can lead to environmental degradation.
items.answer: (a) To reduce inequality in land ownership; to increase production by giving land to those who farm it; to reduce rural poverty and conflict; to correct historical injustices such as colonial land seizure. (b) Tenants and squatters have little incentive to invest in long-term improvements such as terraces or trees; they maximise short-term output; land may be overused.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the problems of land reform. (b) Explain how insecure land tenure can lead to environmental degradation.
items.answer: (a) Resistance from landowners; lack of credit, seeds and skills for new owners; falling output during transition; corruption and elite capture; plots too small; compensation costs. (b) Tenants and squatters have little incentive to invest in long-term improvements such as terraces or trees; they maximise short-term output; land may be overused.

items.stem: “Land reform is the most effective way of improving rural livelihoods.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to support services, tenure and productivity.
items.answer: For: Redistribution reduces inequality and poverty (Taiwan and South Korea after 1950, China’s Household Responsibility System raised output); secure tenure encourages investment. Against: Reform without credit, inputs and markets can fail (Zimbabwe); infrastructure, education, irrigation, microfinance and non-farm jobs may matter more. Conclusion: Land reform can be powerful but works only as part of a package of rural development policies.

items.answer: Monoculture

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the social impacts of agricultural change in rural areas. (b) A student writes: “Agricultural change has only negative impacts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Fewer jobs and rural depopulation; growth of larger farms; rising inequality; debt for inputs; changing gender roles; loss of traditional knowledge; better incomes for some. (b) Not correct. It has raised food production and incomes for many.
items.markingKey: (a) [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A revision website states: “Fertiliser use always raises yields in proportion to the amount applied.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the concept of diminishing returns in fertiliser use.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Returns diminish at higher application rates. (b) At first, extra fertiliser raises yields greatly, but each further increment adds less, until the crop cannot use more and excess is lost to water.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [2]

items.answer: Subsidised fertiliser prices; lack of soil testing and advice; insurance against poor soils; belief that more is better.

Table 18.2 shows the results of a fertiliser trial on maize in Punjab, India (nitrogen applied in kg/ha, yield in t/ha): 0 kg: 3 t, 50 kg: 5.2 t, 100 kg: 6.2 t, 150 kg: 6.6 t, 200 kg: 6.8 t, 250 kg: 6.9 t. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in yield from 0 to 250 kg/ha. (b) Use the data to explain the idea of diminishing returns.
items.answer: (a) +130% (b) Each extra 50 kg adds less yield, falling from 2.2 t to 0.1 t, as other factors such as water, other nutrients and the crop’s genetic potential become limiting.

items.answer: (a) +162.1% (b) Unused nitrate leaches into groundwater and rivers, causing eutrophication and contaminating drinking water; nitrous oxide emissions; soil acidification.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “Crop Intensification Programme (CIP)”?
options: A guaranteed price paid by the government for crops such as wheat and rice in India.
Farmers on neighbouring plots growing the same selected crop to gain economies of scale while keeping ownership.
Rwanda’s programme from 2007 combining land-use consolidation, improved seeds, fertiliser and extension services.
Advice and training for farmers on new methods and technology.
items.answer: Rwanda’s programme from 2007 combining land-use consolidation, improved seeds, fertiliser and extension services.

items.stem: Briefly evaluate the success of the management of agricultural change, for Rwanda (Crop Intensification Programme) or another example of the management of agricultural change in one country.
items.answer: Rwanda (Crop Intensification Programme): Large rises in yields and production of target crops and better food security indicators; but loss of crop diversity, some farmers forced to grow unsuitable crops, unequal benefits and dependence on subsidised inputs.

items.stem: “The management of agricultural change has benefited richer farmers more than poorer farmers.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to inequality and land tenure.
items.answer: For: Green Revolution inputs favoured farmers with land, irrigation and credit; subsidies and support prices benefit larger producers; land consolidation can marginalise smallholders. Against: Doi Moi and China’s reforms reduced rural poverty widely; extension and subsidised inputs in Rwanda reached smallholders; consumers benefited from lower prices. Conclusion: Richer farmers usually gain first and most, but well-designed policies can spread benefits widely.
